Customer requested a 24h dedicated stress benchmark using their prompt corpus and wants security docs and pricing options before committing to a POC.
transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE); Marcus Li (Redwood SE); Priya Nair (BlueWave Eng Mgr); Omar Haddad (BlueWave Platform Eng); Sofia Ruiz (BlueWave SRE); Daniel Kim (BlueWave CTO)
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/decks/edge-case-demo (deck), drive:drive.google.com/bluewave-sample-prompts.xlsx, perf spreadsheet placeholder rwd-bench_v2.xlsx

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
- Ran live API console and backend logs to demonstrate streaming under load.
- Showed a canary that fell back to 1/2-precision quantized model when mem saturated.
- Demonstrated backpressure: client-side 100ms keepalive and server-side 503s during spike; we walked through retry semantics.

Transcript Body:
[00:00:00] Lena: Alright, hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Lena from Redwood, AE on this account. Marcus from our SE team is with me. Quick roll call?
[00:00:10] Marcus: Hey all — Marcus Li, platform SE. I'll drive the demo, show the console and the load harness.
[00:00:18] Priya: Priya here — product and eng manager for the NLP team at BlueWave.
[00:00:22] Omar: Omar, Platform Eng. I'll be focused on network and VPC questions.
[00:00:25] Sofia: Sofia — SRE. Latency SLOs are the thing I'm worried about.
[00:00:30] Daniel: Daniel, CTO. I'm mostly here to listen and make sure we can get an enterprise path.
[00:00:35] Lena: Great. Agenda: quick context (2–3 min), live console demo for long-context + streaming while we spin up a sustained TPS load (about 20–25 min), then logs/traces to show what backpressure looks like, and finish with Q&A and next steps.
[00:01:05] Marcus: Ok starting the console. I'll kick off a long-context session first — we're using a synthetic prompt bundle that imitates your clinical summarization flow — note: this is synthetic, not PII. I'm opening the session with a 120k token prime to simulate prior context.
[00:01:25] Marcus: (typing) console: create session; model: rwd-m-13b-llong (we show a model variant). Streaming toggled on with chunk size 512 tokens.
[00:01:40] Priya: Quick question — your docs mention 250k windows; is that mainline or experimental?
[00:01:48] Marcus: It's supported on dedicated and private deployments with the longcontext kernel; for hosted there's a soft cap but we can accept up to ~250k using streaming KV shards. On hosted, we recommend you pin to a dedicated if you need consistent SLOs at that size.
[00:02:10] Omar: What's the memory footprint? Our infra has mixed A100 and H100 nodes.
[00:02:18] Marcus: For H100 on dedicated with quant-8x you'll see about 60% less memory compared to fp16; kernels differ. The runtime will select kernels at load time — on H100 we use tile-optimized attention which reduces peak KV by ~25%.
[00:02:42] [00:02:42] Marcus: Ok, spinning up the load harness now to ramp to 350 TPS steady.
[00:02:48] [00:02:48] System: load-harness started, target 350 TPS, ramp 30s, duration 20m.
[00:02:55] Sofia: Are you simulating mixed short and long sessions? Our traffic is 70% short (<=1k tokens) and 30% long tails.
[00:03:02] Marcus: Yep — using a distribution file you provided as a template, mixing 70/30. For the long sessions we inject a 120k-250k prefix with KV warm/cold transitions.
[00:03:20] Marcus: Streaming responses are now flowing in the console, you'll see SSE events every 400ms or so. Note that the SSE framing sometimes gets aggregated by proxies — if you're doing gRPC or websocket we recommend keepalive pings at 15s.
[00:03:38] Priya: We're mostly websocket clients. Do you have any known websocket fragmentation issues when tokens per second spike?
[00:03:46] Marcus: Good q. We saw fragmentation on some older ingress controllers. For hosted we use an upgraded edge that handles large frame windows; in Private/VPC you need to tune the ALB/nginx buffer sizes — we can share exact config. I'll drop a link in the notes.
[00:04:05] [00:04:05] Marcus: Alright at ~5 minutes in we're approaching 300 TPS sustained — console shows 95th latency per token at ~38ms, P50 about 12ms.
[00:04:18] Omar: That 95th looks fine but we care about tail for long sessions — what's the per-session end-to-end?
[00:04:24] Marcus: End-to-end for long session paths can hit second-level latencies on tail due to KV cache misses and longer decode loops. We mitigate with prefix caching, sharded KV and early batching to prefetch KVs.
[00:04:42] [00:04:42] System: one worker reported out-of-memory in pod rwd-srv-11; fallback triggered to rwd-m-7b-quant variant for that session (automatic fallback policy: memory_fallback -> smaller_model_variant).
[00:04:55] Priya: We see that — the console annotated the fallback. Does fallback change the token quality deterministically? We can't afford hallucination spikes.
[00:05:03] Marcus: Fallback to smaller variant will change generation characteristics — that's why we recommend A/B thresholds: route only experimental traffic to fallback or allow deterministic reroute rules, plus realtime QA checks. The Optimize tool can score outputs against a golden prompt set to detect regressions.
[00:05:23] Sofia: I'm worried about 503s — what happens to streaming clients when an instance returns transient 503 due to backpressure?
[00:05:30] Marcus: We return a non-200 SSE control event, and client should implement an idempotent resume flow — we provide a small SDK helper that resumes with a resumed_prefix_id to continue generation mid-stream. The default retry window is 10s with exponential backoff; for strict SLOs we suggest client-side hedging across two regions.
[00:05:50] Daniel: Are retries counted double against quota?
[00:05:53] Marcus: Retries are metered as tokens consumed by successful decode attempts. We can instrument a proxy-level dedupe if you want to avoid duplicate billing for retried tokens, but by default tokens generated and streamed are billed.
[00:06:08] Lena: Quick interjection — on pricing we'll include a hedging/overage note and guidance on how to minimize retries via smaller chunk sizes and prefetch.
[00:06:18] [00:06:18] Marcus: Ok ramping to a spike window: an artificial surge to 700 TPS for 60s. Watch the cluster autoscaler and console events.
[00:06:25] [00:06:25] System: cluster-autoscaler request: scale +6 replicas; policy: gentle-scale; predicted spinup 45s.
[00:06:35] Priya: Will autoscaling cause session re-sharding or KV invalidations?
[00:06:39] Marcus: The runtime rebalances by redirecting new sessions to new pods. Existing KV caches are sticky per-pod; we replicate hot prefixes across a small number of pods to avoid cold starts but there is some warming cost. For consistent long-context you want fewer evictions and slightly overprovisioned pools.
[00:06:58] Omar: Can we pin sessions to GPU node groups?
[00:07:02] Marcus: Yes — with Dedicated you can pin to a node pool or affinity group to keep warm caches. Private on-prem also supports node pinning.
[00:07:10] [00:07:10] System: during spike, 3 pods reported elevated queue times; two sessions returned transient stream-control 503s; client SDK retried, resumed via resume token.
[00:07:22] Sofia: In our case even a one-second hiccup is seen as outage. How do we signal degraded mode to clients gracefully?
[00:07:29] Marcus: We recommend a graceful degradation pattern: stream a short system message early (within 200ms) that indicates degraded mode and a fallback token budget; then continue with prioritized tokens. Also route low-criticality requests to a cheaper model variant automatically.
[00:07:47] Priya: Let's talk timeouts — what is the recommended idle timeout for long streaming sessions behind a corporate proxy?
[00:07:55] Marcus: For websockets we recommend 90–120s keepalive; for SSE we prefer 60s and use periodic noop frames. If proxies have 30s idle timeouts you'll need to push keepalives more frequently.
[00:08:12] Marcus: Switching to logs/traces now — per-request trace shows KV cache hit/miss, decode loop time, and kernel selection. I'm opening a trace for a session that experienced a fallback earlier.
[00:08:25] [00:08:25] Marcus: Trace: request 0x7af3. KV hit-rate 0.73 for the first 30k tokens then drop to 0.2 after a shard rotation. Kernel selected: h100_tile_attention_v2. Decode latency per token averages 14ms, spikes to 320ms on certain long tokens due to attention recompute.
[00:08:50] Daniel: That attention recompute — can it be avoided with quantization or is that orthogonal?
[00:08:56] Marcus: Quantization reduces memory and sometimes reduces attention recompute cost because we can use different kernel permutations, but some recomputes are algorithmic (like when sequence length crosses a boundary and we need to reshuffle KV slices). We have a planned optimization to reduce that boundary cost by preallocating lanes.
[00:09:16] Priya: Are you able to provide a per-token latency breakdown by model variant for our expected prompt distribution?
[00:09:22] Marcus: Yes — we'll produce a per-variant CSV as part of the benchmark. That's part of the 24h run.
[00:09:30] [00:09:30] System: load harness steady at ~350 TPS for 12 minutes now. We see a periodic jitter correlated with GC cycles on some pods.
[00:09:40] Sofia: GC cycles — can you tune the runtime GC or is it fixed?
[00:09:44] Marcus: There's GC tuning knobs. On dedicated you can set the memory_gc_threshold and enable soft-reclaim settings. With GPU memory managers newer drivers reduce CPU-side jitter. We'll share recommended defaults.
[00:09:58] Lena: Quick question from pricing — if we go Dedicated with reserved capacity what's the minimum commit for a 250k-context SLA?
[00:10:05] Marcus: It depends on throughput targets, but ballpark for enterprise SLAs with 250k context we recommend a baseline of two H100-like pods reserved and a burst pool. We'll have finance provide exact numbers.
[00:10:20] [00:10:20] System: simulated client connection drop (client-proxy timeout) for session 0x9f22; resume attempted.
[00:10:28] Marcus: Resume succeeded for that session using session_resume_id. Client dropped and reconnected within 6s.
[00:10:34] Priya: You mentioned earlier a 'resume token' — is that opaque or verifiable by client?
[00:10:40] Marcus: It's opaque but signed; the server verifies it on resume. We can optionally return a resume-proof for audit use.
[00:10:50] [00:10:50] Marcus: Jumping ahead — here's the Optimize tab where we show quality regressions; we ran a quick eval on a small prompt set and scored BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics and a custom hallucination score. You can hook your golden set and we'll run daily regression alerts.
[00:11:12] Priya: That's helpful. The hallucination detector — how false-positive heavy is it?
[00:11:18] Marcus: It's tuned conservatively; you'll get fewer false positives but may miss subtle factual drift. We recommend pairing with human review on flagged hits.
[00:11:28] [00:11:28] System: autoscaler finished spinup; new replicas are warmed. Cluster CPU stable.
[00:11:35] Marcus: Now we're going to exercise a longer tail: simulate a 250k token session with occasional short bursts (10–20 TPS) while we keep cluster under moderate load.
[00:11:50] [00:11:50] Marcus: Long session streaming now — you'll see progressive token streaming. Note the KV warm step takes about ~6–8s on initial decode.
[00:11:58] Priya: That warm step — can we prewarm using an async prefetch at session start?
[00:12:04] Marcus: Yes. We support an async prefetch API call that fetches prefixes and warms KVs without starting generation; it's cheap and recommended for long sessions.
[00:12:14] Omar: Does prefetch count toward billing?
[00:12:17] Marcus: Prefetch is metered lightly — we charge a small fixed cost per prefetch and not per token, but we'll itemize it in the pricing doc.
[00:12:27] [00:12:27] System: one long session hit a 120s proxy idle timeout and the client connection was severed; we persisted resume token.
[00:12:36] Sofia: That proxy timeout is exactly the problem we wanted to catch. If our proxies drop at 120s, people on long sessions will disconnect — what are options?
[00:12:43] Marcus: Options: increase keepalive frequency; use a two-phase model where initial heavy compute returns an early summary and continues background work via async job; or use chunked transcripts with periodic checkpoints persisted to object store so the client can re-hydrate.
[00:13:00] Priya: What's the easiest to implement from our side?
[00:13:03] Marcus: Keepalives are easiest. Next best is chunked transcripts with resume tokens; we have SDK helpers for both.
[00:13:12] [00:13:12] Marcus: Ok shifting to failover and routing — here's the policy editor in Console. You can set route by latency, cost, or region. You can also configure automatic fallbacks to a quantized variant if memory_fallback triggers.
[00:13:28] Priya: Can the policy be per-customer or per-route? We have multiple product teams that need different tradeoffs.
[00:13:33] Lena: Yes, routes are per-API-key and you can attach policies at route-level. The Console shows route-level metrics and cost breakdowns.
[00:13:45] [00:13:45] Marcus: I'm going to show a demo of backpressure in slow-path: artificially reduce available GPU memory on one group to force backpressure.
[00:13:55] [00:13:55] System: mem-pressure injected on node-group-3; queue depth increases; streaming latency climbs.
[00:14:05] Marcus: See that? The consumer saw an SSE 'degraded' event and we routed lower-critical requests to a smaller model.
[00:14:12] Omar: Is there an alert channel integration? We use PagerDuty.
[00:14:16] Marcus: Yep — Slack, PagerDuty, Datadog, and you can webhook into any incident system.
[00:14:22] [00:14:22] System: after mitigation, mem-pressure relieved by scale-up.
[00:14:28] Priya: Anything else we should be careful about for VPC/private deployments?
[00:14:32] Marcus: Network egress, private peering, and KMS integration are the three big ones. For HSM/KMS you need key wrapping policies and we recommend bringing your own key for compliance. Also sidecar configs for large frame handling on your ingress.
[00:14:49] [00:14:49] Daniel: On SOC2 and audit logs — we need proof that gen requests and audit trails are retained for 12 months with redaction.
[00:14:56] Lena: We'll include the SOC2 summary and an audit-log sample showing redaction features in the security pack.
[00:15:05] [00:15:05] Marcus: Ok we're at ~20 minutes into the load; cluster stabilizing at 380 TPS. I'm going to run a short test that forces a streaming timeout mid-generation to show resume semantics.
[00:15:18] [00:15:18] System: simulate stream error (proxy 504) at 00:15:18 for session 0xC11; SDK attempts resume.
[00:15:26] Priya: The SDK auto-resumed — can we get logs that show resumed payloads separately?
[00:15:31] Marcus: Yes, Console shows resume events and diffs; you can query via API: /v1/sessions/:id/events.
[00:15:40] [00:15:40] Marcus: I'm going to flip to a short demo: showing how Optimize suggests batching knobs. For your workload, with 70/30 split, it recommended a batch_target_tokens of 2k and max_batch_delay 25ms to balance latency and cost.
[00:15:58] Priya: Those knobs — are they cluster-level or per-route?
[00:16:02] Marcus: Per-route and you can also set pool-level defaults. We deploy a smart-batcher that adapts to incoming qps and token lengths.
[00:16:10] [00:16:10] System: small regression detected by Optimize on golden-set prompt #23 — hallucination score increase 0.08.
[00:16:18] Lena: We'll include the Optimize diff in the benchmark output and point to possible model swap or quant config to mitigate.
[00:16:28] Priya: Cool. Let's talk about SLA during a POC; we want a 99.9% per-route uptime and tail latency < 2s for short sessions. Any redlines?
[00:16:38] Marcus: For short sessions that's achievable on Dedicated with reserved capacity and burst buffers. Long sessions are a different class — tail may be higher due to KV shuffles. We'll map specific SLOs in the POC scoping doc.
[00:16:52] [00:16:52] System: load harness starting cool-down phase.
[00:16:58] Marcus: Quick pause — questions from the team?
[00:17:05] Omar: On the private deployment side, what sort of ops footprint would we need for a 24/7 POC?
[00:17:11] Marcus: Expect a small ops rotation to handle scale events; our private package includes an ops playbook and runbook — typically 1-2 engineers on call during POC.
[00:17:24] Sofia: What observability retention do you ship by default? We need 90 days at minimum.
[00:17:29] Lena: Default is 30 days; enterprise add-on supports 90/365 day retention for traces and logs.
[00:17:36] [00:17:36] Marcus: Ok final demo piece: burst recovery. I'll kill two pods to simulate failure and watch session recovery.
[00:17:44] [00:17:44] System: pod rwd-srv-7 terminated; 2 sessions failed over to new pods; resume tokens used to rehydrate stream; one session saw a short gap of ~1.2s.
[00:17:58] Priya: That 1.2s gap — acceptable, but in some flows that's visible to end user. The resume pattern seems solid though.
[00:18:05] Daniel: Are there options to hide the gap with client-side buffering?
[00:18:09] Marcus: Yes — buffer on client and replay system messages; or apply a 'grace window' that fills with a placeholder then merges with resumed content.
[00:18:19] [00:18:19] Marcus: We're wrapping up the live demo. Summary of findings seen live: 1) autoscaler works but warm/cold KV transitions create tail spikes; 2) stream resume works, but proxies and idle timeouts need tuning; 3) fallback to smaller models is automatic but affects quality — watch with Optimize.
[00:18:45] Priya: This was useful. Next steps — we'll share logs and a sanitized prompt set. We want Redwood to run the 24h bench and produce per-variant CSVs and a short recommendations doc.
[00:18:56] Lena: Yep, action items noted. Marcus will run the bench and produce the spreadsheet; Lena will send security+pricing.
[00:19:06] Priya: Timeline expectations? If we provide prompts by Thursday, when can we expect the benchmark?
[00:19:12] Marcus: If prompts by Thursday (2026-12-16), bench results by Friday (2026-12-17) EOD. We'll also include a follow-up call on Monday 2026-12-18.
[00:19:23] Daniel: Good. Also cc me on the SOC2 and contract skeleton.
[00:19:29] Lena: Will do.
[00:19:33] [00:19:33] System: call recording ended.
